title: Probabilistic SLI mapping and surge eviction guidelines
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Objective: Define a probabilistic approach to map per-endpoint and per-model SLIs into composite error budgets, and produce operational guidelines for surge eviction (load shedding) and regional circuit-breaker policies. The goal is to reduce unnecessary failovers and throttling during transient spikes while preserving SLOs for high-priority routes.

Scope:
- Per-endpoint SLIs: latency (p50/p95/p99), correctness (semantic match rate), and availability (5xx/timeout rates).
- Per-model adjustments: account for model size, kv-cache hit rate, and known cold-start characteristics.
- Composite SLOs: weighted, probabilistic aggregation (see algorithm section) that produces a posterior distribution for budget consumption rather than a single point estimate.
- Surge eviction: define step-down eviction policies that use probabilistic signals + short-term burst tokens to avoid oscillation.
- Circuit breakers: regional and model-variant breakers with decaying token buckets and Bayesian confidence thresholds.

Deliverables:
1) SLI mapping algorithm spec (Bayesian weighting and posterior error budget allocation).
2) A decision matrix for surge eviction per customer tier/route/model.
3) Circuit breaker config templates (per-region and per-variant) and recommended default thresholds.
4) Incident runbook with escalation and automated fallback checks.
5) Prototype telemetry dashboard queries and alerts.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Why probabilistic? Fixed thresholds cause brittle behavior when traffic is bursty or telemetry is sparse. A posterior distribution gives us uncertainty bands to avoid knee-jerk evictions.
- Weighting strategy: routes with financial or safety impact (billing, auth) receive higher weight; internal low-impact routes get lower weight. We will cap any single route's influence to prevent domination.
- Complexity vs. operability: the model must be auditable and debuggable by on-call. We limit model complexity (no deep ML) and provide visualizations for the posterior.
- Cost: more sophisticated SLI math increases CPU for evaluation; we will sample windows and only update full posterior every 30s by default.

Algorithm (high-level):
- For each route r and model m, compute per-window SLI observations: latency percentiles, 5xx rate, semantic-error rate.
- Convert observations into a likelihood for meeting the route-level SLO.
- Maintain a conjugate prior (beta for rates, normal-inverse-gamma for latencies) to produce a posterior probability that the route is violating SLO.
- Aggregate across routes with weights w(r,m) to produce a composite posterior for model endpoints.
- Error budget spend is then expressed as a distribution; automated policies act when P(violation) > threshold T_high for sustained duration or when expected remaining budget falls below dynamic floor.

Surge eviction policy (summary):
- Stage 0 (pre-eviction): apply soft throttles and prefer cheaper model variants (quantized or smaller) if available.
- Stage 1 (controlled eviction): apply token-bucket based eviction by route priority; high-priority routes get burst tokens, low-priority routes are shed first.
- Stage 2 (regional isolation): if a region's composite posterior exceeds emergency threshold and autoscaling cannot recover, start diverting low-priority traffic to fallback regions or model variants.
- Rehydration: evicted routes enter a cooldown with exponentially increasing backoff windows to prevent flapping.

Circuit breaker guidelines:
- Two axes: confidence (posterior probability) and velocity (rate of change). We open a breaker when high confidence + high velocity are present.
- Use decaying token-buckets so that small failures are retried, but sustained failures trigger open state.
- Per-variant breakers: heavier models get less aggressive breakers to protect capacity; cheaper variants can be used as fallback.

Operational runbook (incident playflow):
- Alert triggers: composite P(violation) > 0.9 for 3 consecutive windows OR expected budget < 10% within next 1h.
- On-call first responder: check dashboard panel (link below) for contributing routes and models; identify whether the issue is traffic surge, model degradation, or infra.
- If surge: enable soft-throttles and switch low-priority routes to cheaper variants.
- If infra (GPU / network): initiate regional circuit-breaker and begin routing to reserve region; fire a PagerDuty SE escalation.
- Post-incident: capture learning in incident doc, update priors if system behavior has changed, and schedule follow-up (see comments).

Links:
- Confluence spec (draft): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUN/Probabilistic+SLI+Mapping
- Prototype dashboard (Grafana): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/SLI/probabilistic-sli-overview
- GitHub prototype PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1821

Open questions:
- Should we expose the composite posterior to customers in Console or only surface a simplified SLO status? (PM/Legal input required)
- Default thresholds: T_high=0.95 is proposed but may be tweaked after chaos testing.
- How to incorporate cost signals (spot vs reserved GPUs) into weighting?

next_steps: Complete internal chaos test (simulate bursty traffic + region eviction) by 2025-02-25; iterate thresholds based on false-positive rate; implement circuit-breaker templates and land runtime defaults in runtime-1.20 branch.
acceptance_criteria: 1) Prototype produces stable posterior with <5% variance over 5 runs in baseline traffic. 2) Surge eviction shields top-3 priority routes while keeping 70% of low-priority requests served under sustained 3x baseline traffic. 3) Circuit breaker templates validated in canary region with automated rollback.
